a: at the season when kings march out
p: Armies marched in spring, after the winter rains and before the harvest called men home.
b: Ancient Near Eastern kings usually went to war in spring. The winter rains were over, roads were passable, and the grain in the fields could feed an army on the move. Assyrian royal records count campaigns year by year in the same way. The sentence sets up a contrast that the narrator never states outright: this is the season when kings go out, and King David stays home. The war with Ammon began in chapter 10, and this verse picks it up again. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, lies under modern Amman in Jordan.

a: But David was staying in Jerusalem
t: Was David wrong to stay home?
p: The text does not say staying home was a sin, but readers have long heard a quiet judgment in it.
b: Nothing in the law required a king to lead every campaign, and later the army itself asks David to stay behind (18:3; 21:17). Some readers, Jewish and Christian, take the verse at face value: a king in his fifties could leave a siege to his general. Most literary readers (the L lens) hear irony: "kings march out" and David "was staying," the same verb used of the ark and the army living in shelters in 11:11. The idle king on the roof stands in contrast to the soldier who will not even go home to sleep. The narrator lets the contrast speak without comment.

a: walking about on the roof of the king's house
p: Flat roofs were living space. A palace on a ridge looked down into courtyards below.
b: Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs used for sleeping, drying produce and cool evening air (1 Samuel 9:25–26; Joshua 2:6). David's palace, built by Hiram's craftsmen (5:11), stood on the high point of the old city, so its roof looked down into the courtyards of the houses around it. Bathsheba was probably washing in an enclosed courtyard, not in public. Excavations on the ridge of the City of David have uncovered a large stone structure that Eilat Mazar identified as David's palace; many archaeologists date it differently or question the identification.

a: the woman was very lovely to look at
p: The same praise is given to Rebekah, Rachel, Abigail and Esther. Beauty in Samuel often brings danger.
b: Hebrew tovat mar'eh me'od is literally "good of appearance, very." The phrase praises Rebekah (Genesis 24:16) and Queen Vashti (Esther 1:11; compare Esther 2:7), and similar words describe Rachel, Abigail (1 Samuel 25:3) and Tamar (13:1). In the books of Samuel, the good-looking are often in danger or dangerous: David himself (1 Samuel 16:12), Tamar, Absalom (14:25). The narrator gives only what David sees. Bathsheba's thoughts are never told.

a: Bathsheba, Eliam's daughter, the wife of Uriah the Hittite
p: Her father and husband were both among David's elite warriors, and her grandfather may have been Ahithophel.
b: The answer David gets is a warning in itself: she is a married woman, and her family is close to the throne. An Eliam son of Ahithophel and Uriah the Hittite are both listed among David's Thirty, his elite fighters (23:34, 39). If this Eliam is the same man, Bathsheba was the granddaughter of Ahithophel, David's counselor, who later joins Absalom's revolt (15:12). The Talmud makes that link (Sanhedrin 69b). 1 Chronicles 3:5 calls her Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel, a different spelling of both names (Eliam and Ammiel use the same two parts in reverse order).

a: Uriah the Hittite
p: Uriah, a Hittite, bears a Hebrew name: "the LORD is my light." He may be a foreigner who worships Israel's God.
b: "Hittites" in the Bible are usually one of the peoples of Canaan (Genesis 23; Deuteronomy 7:1), probably related to the Neo-Hittite city-states of Syria in this period. Uriah's name, Uriyyah, means "the LORD is my light" or "my light is the LORD," which suggests that he or his parents worshiped Israel's God. He lives in Jerusalem near the palace and is listed among David's Thirty (23:39). The story places a loyal foreigner beside an Israelite king who breaks faith, as the book does again with Ittai the Gittite (15:19–21).

a: David sent messengers and took her
p: The verbs belong to David: he sent, took, lay. Readers differ over how much choice Bathsheba had.
b: Three readings stand out. (1) Complicit. A few modern readers, notably George Nicol, suggest she bathed where she knew the king could see, or later used her position shrewdly (1 Kings 1). Randall Bailey reads the match as a political alliance with an influential family. (2) Victim of a king's power. Others, including Richard Davidson and Cheryl Exum, stress that David "sent" and "took" (laqach), that no one refuses a king's summons, and that Nathan's parable blames only the rich man: the lamb does nothing. Many call it rape by abuse of power. (3) A silent character. Literary readers (Meir Sternberg, Gale Yee) note that the narrator deliberately withholds her motives. She speaks only two Hebrew words in the whole chapter: "I'm pregnant" (11:5). All three readings agree that the text and Nathan hold David responsible.

a: She had been purifying herself from her uncleanness
t: Why the narrator mentions her purification
p: Her washing marked the end of her monthly period. So she was not already pregnant, and the child could only be David's.
b: The Hebrew mitqaddeshet mittum'atah, "making herself holy from her uncleanness," points to the purity laws: after her period a woman counted seven days and then washed (Leviticus 15:19, 28; the washing itself is assumed there and spelled out in later Jewish law). The detail explains the bath of 11:2 and closes a door: since she had just had her period, Uriah, away at war, cannot be the father. Some read the clause as happening during the visit; most take it as background ("she had been purifying herself"). The irony is sharp: she is carefully keeping the purity law while David breaks the commandment against adultery (Exodus 20:14).

a: I'm pregnant
p: In Hebrew her only speech in the chapter is two words, harah anokhi.
b: Harah anokhi, "pregnant I," is all that Bathsheba says until 1 Kings 1. The short message puts the problem squarely back on David, who now acts with growing speed: three times in quick succession he "sends" (11:6, 11:14, 11:27). The verb "send" (shalach) runs through the chapter about a dozen times, and the one who sends is always the one with power. Bathsheba sends only once, and only to report what has happened to her body.

a: the army's well-being and the war's well-being
p: David asks about the shalom, the peace, of a war. The odd phrase hints that his questions are a cover.
b: Hebrew asks after someone's shalom, "peace, welfare," as a greeting. David asks three times: Joab's shalom, the army's shalom, "the war's shalom." Asking about the peace of a war is a strange phrase, and many readers hear the narrator smiling at a king making small talk while he plans something else. Uriah's answer is not recorded.

a: wash your feet
p: On the surface an invitation to rest after a journey; many also hear a hint at sleeping with his wife.
b: Washing the feet was what a traveler did on arriving home (Genesis 18:4; 43:24). In Hebrew "feet" can also be a polite word for the private parts (Ruth 3:7; Isaiah 7:20), so many interpreters think David's order carries a hint. Uriah answers both meanings in 11:11 by naming exactly what he will not do: eat, drink and lie with his wife. The gift that followed him is literally "the king's portion" (mas'at hammelekh), probably food from the royal table.

a: The ark, Israel and Judah are living in shelters
t: The ark at the front, and soldiers' purity
p: The ark went to war with the army, and soldiers on campaign kept away from women.
b: The ark of the covenant could be carried into battle (1 Samuel 4:3–4), and here it is camped with the army at Rabbah. The "shelters" (sukkot) are field huts of branches, like those of the Feast of Booths. Some scholars (Yigael Yadin) suggest instead the town of Succoth across the Jordan, a staging base for the war. Soldiers on campaign were to stay away from sex (1 Samuel 21:5; Deuteronomy 23:9–14), so Uriah's refusal is a soldier's piety, and David knows the rule. Whether Uriah suspected what had happened is a gap the text leaves open.

a: I swear by your life, by your very self, I will not do it!
p: The narrator does not tell us. The question changes how Uriah's refusal reads.
b: Meir Sternberg's study of this chapter made it a classic example of the Bible's deliberate "gaps." If Uriah knows nothing, his refusal is simple loyalty, and his goodness shames the king. If he has heard palace gossip (the servants at the gate had seen everything), his refusal is quiet defiance, and his oath by the king's life becomes double-edged. The rabbis took a harsher view of Uriah: in the Talmud (Shabbat 56a) he is called a rebel against the crown for calling Joab "my lord" in the king's presence and refusing the king's order. Most readers today see him as the most upright man in the chapter.

a: David made him drunk
p: David's second trick echoes the daughters of Lot, who also used wine to get around a man's will.
b: Making someone drunk to use him is told of Lot's daughters (Genesis 19:32–35) and condemned in Habakkuk 2:15. Even drunk, Uriah sleeps at the palace door, which some readers take to show that his refusal was a firm decision, not a mood. Absalom will later wait for Amnon's heart to be "feeling good with the wine" before having him killed (13:28): wine at a feast becomes a tool of murder in David's own house.

a: sent it in Uriah's own hand
t: Uriah carries his own death warrant
p: Readers have always noticed the cruelty: Uriah is trusted not to read the letter.
b: The detail assumes either that Uriah could not read or that he would never open a sealed royal letter. The Greek poet Homer tells a similar story of Bellerophon, who carried a sealed message asking the receiver to kill him (Iliad 6.155–211), and "a letter of Uriah" became a proverb in several European languages for a message that harms its bearer. Readers have taken the parallel as a common folk motif, not as borrowing either way. Joab, who receives the letter, now holds a secret over the king; later he will act against David's wishes more than once (18:14; 3:27).

a: Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?
p: Joab expects David to cite a lesson from Judges: never fight too close to a city wall.
b: Abimelech, Gideon's son, was killed while attacking the tower of Thebez when "a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head" (Judges 9:53). Joab expects David to know the story the way soldiers know famous blunders. The irony runs deeper: Abimelech, like David, died because of a woman, and the citation slips a woman into the battle report just as Bathsheba lies behind Uriah's death. "Jerubbesheth" is Gideon's other name Jerubbaal with "Baal" replaced by boshet, "shame," as in Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth (see the variant).

a: Do not let this thing look evil in your eyes
t: "Evil in your eyes" and "evil in the LORD's eyes"
p: David tells Joab not to see the deaths as evil. Two verses later the LORD sees what David did as evil.
b: Hebrew al yera be'eyneykha et haddavar hazzeh is literally "let this thing not be evil in your eyes," a common idiom for "don't be upset." The narrator uses the same words for the chapter's only judgment: "what David had done looked evil in the LORD's eyes" (11:27). Most English versions flatten the link by using different words in the two places. The Plain English keeps the same image so the reader can hear the narrator's verdict answering the king's.

a: The sword eats one man now and another man then
p: Hebrew pictures the sword with a mouth. David's shrug about chance in war will come back to him in 12:10.
b: "The sword devours" is a stock Hebrew image (2:26; Deuteronomy 32:42); a sword's edge is literally its "mouth." David's line sounds like soldiers' fatalism: in war, anyone may fall. Nathan answers with the same noun: "the sword will not go away from your house, ever" (12:10). The sword that David treats as random in 11:25 becomes, in Nathan's word, the LORD's judgment on his own family.

a: she wailed for her husband
p: The narrator calls her "Uriah's wife" and Uriah "her husband" three times in one verse.
b: The Hebrew verb safad means to wail or beat the breast in public mourning. Whether her grief was deep or formal is not said. The narrator does not call her Bathsheba here, but "Uriah's wife," and names Uriah "her husband" twice; Matthew's genealogy still calls her "the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6). The usual mourning period was seven days (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13), so the marriage followed quickly, perhaps quickly enough to hide the timing of the birth.

a: But what David had done looked evil in the LORD's eyes
p: For the first time in the David story, the LORD is said to be displeased with David.
b: Until now the narrator has repeated that "the LORD was with" David (1 Samuel 18:14; 2 Samuel 5:10). Here, in the last line of the chapter, the LORD appears only to judge. Critical scholars (the C lens) see this verse and Nathan's speech in chapter 12 as places where a theological editor framed an older court story; others think the court story itself was written by someone who saw history under God's judgment. Both agree that this sentence turns the whole book: from here the sword, the rape, the murder and the revolt follow.

a: So the LORD sent Nathan to David
p: All through chapter 11 David "sent." Chapter 12 opens with the LORD sending.
b: The verb shalach, "send," was David's in chapter 11: he sent for information, for Bathsheba, for Uriah, for the letter, and finally for Bathsheba again (11:27). Now the sender is the LORD, and the one sent is Nathan, the prophet who had brought David the promise of a lasting house (7:4–17). The king who has been moving people like pieces on a board is now on the receiving end. Nathan reappears at Solomon's birth (12:25) and in the struggle over the succession (1 Kings 1).

a: Two men lived in one town. One was rich, the other poor.
t: A trap made of a story
p: Nathan's tale is a "juridical parable": a made-up legal case that tricks the hearer into judging himself.
b: Uriel Simon called this a juridical parable. A realistic case is brought to the king as if it were a real lawsuit, the king gives his ruling, and then the speaker reveals that the case was about the king. The same pattern appears in the wise woman of Tekoa's story (14:1–20), the prophet's disguise before Ahab (1 Kings 20:35–43), and Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). It works only if the hearer does not see himself in the story. David, who as king judged such cases (15:2–4), condemns himself before he knows it. Jesus' parables sometimes work the same way (Matthew 21:33–45; Luke 7:40–47).

a: To him it was like a daughter
p: The Hebrew for daughter is bat, the first part of Bathsheba's name. Many readers hear a pointer.
b: The lamb is "like a daughter" (kevat), and it "lay in his lap" (becheqo), the same word Nathan uses when God gave David his master's wives "into your lap" (12:8). Readers since the Middle Ages have heard Bath-sheba, "daughter of Sheba" or "daughter of an oath," behind the lamb, and Uriah behind the poor man who "had nothing at all but" her. The parable is not an exact allegory: the rich man kills the lamb, while David killed the husband. The fit is close enough to catch David, loose enough that he does not notice.

a: One day a visitor dropped in on the rich man
p: The visitor is called a traveler, a guest and "the man who had come." The rabbis read it as desire growing.
b: Hebrew calls him first a helekh, "one who is walking, a passer-by," then an oreach, "a traveler, guest," and finally "the man who had come to him." The Talmud (Sukkah 52b) reads this as the evil inclination: at first it is a passer-by, then a guest, and in the end it is master of the house. Whatever one makes of that, the point of the story is the host's greed: hospitality was a duty, and the rich man meets it at a poor man's expense.

a: the man who did this deserves death!
p: David's verdict is literally "a son of death." It means he deserves to die, though sheep theft did not carry death.
b: Hebrew ben mavet, "son of death," means someone who deserves death or is doomed (1 Samuel 20:31; 26:16). Under the law, stealing and slaughtering a sheep was repaid four times over, not by death (Exodus 22:1). David's anger outruns the law, which shows how strongly he feels the cruelty of the act. The irony is that David, under the law, is the one who has earned death twice over, for adultery and for murder (Leviticus 20:10; Exodus 21:12).

a: For the lamb he must repay four lambs
p: David's sentence follows the law of Exodus 22:1. The rabbis counted four of David's children lost.
b: The law says a thief "must repay with five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep" (Exodus 22:1). David rules by the book. The Talmud (Yoma 22b) notes that David himself paid fourfold: the baby (12:18), Amnon (13:29), Tamar, ruined (13:20), and Absalom (18:15). Zacchaeus offers the same fourfold repayment to those he cheated (Luke 19:8). The Greek reads "sevenfold" (see the variant).

a: You are the man!
p: Two Hebrew words, attah ha'ish. A court prophet tells the king to his face that he is the criminal.
b: In the ancient Near East, prophets were usually employed by kings and expected to support them. Nathan's two words, attah ha'ish, are a rare picture of a prophet judging a king by a law the king is also under (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Jewish and Christian readers alike have taken the scene as a model of courage in speaking truth to power: Ambrose of Milan used it when he confronted the emperor Theodosius in AD 390. The phrase also answers 12:5: David called the rich man "the man who did this"; Nathan says "you are the man."

a: put your master's wives into your lap
t: A king inherits his predecessor's wives
p: Taking the harem of the previous king was a claim to his throne. Absalom will use the same move in 16:22.
b: No other passage says David married any of Saul's wives; we know of only Ahinoam and Rizpah (1 Samuel 14:50; 3:7). The words may simply mean that everything Saul had came into David's power. In the ancient Near East, taking over a king's women was a public claim to his kingship. That is why Abner's affair with Rizpah angered Ish-bosheth (3:7), why Absalom lies with David's concubines (16:22), and why Adonijah's request for Abishag cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13–25). The point here is generosity: God gave David more than enough, so he had no need to steal.

a: Why have you despised the word of the LORD
p: The verb bazah repeats in 12:10: to despise God's word is to despise God himself.
b: Hebrew bazah means to treat as worthless. In 12:9 David has despised "the word of the LORD"; in 12:10 the LORD says "you despised me." The same verb described Esau, who "despised" his birthright (Genesis 25:34), and Eli's family, whom the LORD warned that "the ones who scorn me will count for little" (1 Samuel 2:30), where this site renders the same verb "scorn". Psalm 51, which tradition ties to this scene, ends by promising that God will not despise a broken and crushed heart (Psalm 51:17).

a: Him you killed with the sword of the Ammonites
p: Nathan says David killed Uriah, even though Ammonite archers fired the arrows.
b: Nathan names David as the killer twice in one verse: "you struck down" and "you killed." The Ammonite sword was only the tool. Both Jewish and Christian ethics have drawn the principle from this: whoever arranges a death through others carries the guilt. The rabbis who defended David (Shabbat 56a) argued that Uriah was a rebel who deserved death and that David's sin was only in not trying him properly; even they agree that Nathan's charge stands as a charge.

a: So the sword will not go away from your house, ever
p: Three of David's sons die by the sword: Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah.
b: The rest of the book reads like the outworking of this sentence. Amnon is murdered by Absalom's servants (13:28–29), Absalom is killed by Joab (18:14–15), and Adonijah is executed by Solomon (1 Kings 2:25). The sword also strikes outside the family: Amasa is killed by Joab (20:10), and Joab by Solomon's order (1 Kings 2:34). Readers differ on how to understand this. Some take it as a punishment God actively sends. Others read it as the natural harvest of what David taught his household: lust, deceit and violence passed down to his sons. The text holds both together: "I am raising up disaster" (12:11).

a: He will sleep with your wives with this very sun watching
t: Done in secret, repaid in public
p: The punishment fits the crime in reverse: a hidden act answered in full view. It comes true in 16:22.
b: The "someone close to you" (re'akha, "your neighbor, companion") turns out to be David's own son. On Ahithophel's advice, Absalom pitches a tent on the palace roof, the same roof from which David first saw Bathsheba, and goes in to David's concubines "with all Israel watching" (16:22). The sun here is not a god; the phrase means in broad daylight. The structure is measure for measure, a principle both the Bible and the rabbis use often (Judges 1:6–7; Mishnah Sotah 1:7).

a: David said to Nathan
p: The heading of Psalm 51 ties it to this moment. The psalm is David's confession at length.
b: Psalm 51 is headed "For the music director. A psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after David had come to Bathsheba" (Psalm 51:0). The Hebrew plays on one verb, bo, "come, go in": Nathan came to David as David had come to Bathsheba. The psalm prays, "You, you alone, are the one I sinned against; what is evil in your eyes, I did it" (Psalm 51:4), taking up the narrator's verdict of 11:27, and asks, "Create a pure heart for me, O God" (Psalm 51:10) and "your holy spirit, do not take it from me" (Psalm 51:11), perhaps remembering Saul (1 Samuel 16:14). It ends: "A heart broken and crushed, O God, you will not look down on" (Psalm 51:17). The verb there, bazah, is the one translated "despised" in 12:9–10, so the psalm answers that charge. Many scholars date the psalm, or at least its last two verses, later than David; others defend the heading. It has a long place in Jewish and Christian prayers of repentance, and many churches read it on Ash Wednesday.

a: I have sinned against the LORD
p: David's confession is two Hebrew words. Readers compare it with Saul's longer, excuse-filled confession.
b: Hebrew chata'ti laYHWH is just two words. Saul also said "I have sinned" to Samuel, but went on to explain that he feared the people and asked to be honored before the elders (1 Samuel 15:24–30). David offers no excuse and asks for nothing. Jewish tradition holds up this moment as the model of repentance (teshuvah), and some sages say the Bible records David's sin precisely to teach that no one is beyond returning to God (Avodah Zarah 4b–5a). Christians have read it the same way, often with Psalm 51 as David's longer prayer.

a: The LORD, for his part, has put away your sin. You will not die.
t: Forgiven, but not spared the consequences
p: The law demanded death for adultery and murder. God sets aside the death penalty but not every result of the sin.
b: By the law, David deserved to die (Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 35:31). Nathan's word is that the LORD has "caused your sin to pass over" (he'evir), the verb used for God passing by Moses in mercy (Exodus 33:19). Yet the child dies and the sword stays. Interpreters explain this tension in several ways: forgiveness restores the relationship with God but does not undo every consequence in history; David's contempt for the LORD's word needed a visible answer (12:14); or the child's death is not a punishment of the child but a loss to David. Paul quotes another psalm of David on the blessing of the forgiven (Romans 4:6–8; Psalm 32:1–2).

a: the son born to you will surely die
p: Readers have long struggled with a baby dying for his father's sin. The text does not explain it.
b: The law says children must not be put to death for their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Ezekiel insists that each person bears his own guilt (Ezekiel 18:20). Yet here the LORD strikes the child (12:15). Traditional answers: the child is taken to heaven or to rest, and the loss falls on David, not the child (many Christian readers, drawing on 12:23); the death protects God's name, because a child born of adultery and murder could not be the heir (some Jewish commentators). Critical readers note that ancient Israel thought of a family as one body under God, so judgment on a father fell on his house. Many modern readers simply admit that the verse is hard and leave it so.

a: He went without food
p: Fasting while lying on the ground in sackcloth was how Israelites mourned and pleaded with God.
b: Fasting, sleeping on the ground and wearing sackcloth (coarse goat-hair cloth) were signs of grief and of urgent prayer (1 Kings 21:27; Joel 1:13; Jonah 3:5–8). David does them before the child dies, not after, which is the reverse of normal mourning. His servants expect grief to come after the death and are confused when it stops (12:21). His answer in 12:22–23 shows that the fast was prayer, not mourning: while there was hope, he pleaded; when God had answered, he accepted it.

a: He went to the LORD's house and bowed in worship
p: The temple was not built yet. David worships at the tent where the ark stood in Jerusalem.
b: Solomon built the temple later (1 Kings 6). "The LORD's house" here must be the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (6:17), which 1 Samuel also calls a "house" at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:7, 24). David's first act after the child's death is worship. Jewish commentators (Radak) read it as acceptance of God's judgment, the attitude Job expresses: "the LORD gave, and the LORD took" (Job 1:21).

a: Who knows? The LORD might show me favor
p: The same hopeful question is asked by the king of Nineveh and by Joel: God may yet relent.
b: Hebrew mi yodea, "who knows?", expresses hope in God's freedom to change course. The king of Nineveh says it (Jonah 3:9), Joel urges Judah to return with it (Joel 2:14), and Esther's cousin uses it of her becoming queen (Esther 4:14). In David's case the answer was no. The passage shows a faith that both prays boldly and accepts the answer.

a: I am the one who will go to him. He will not come back to me.
p: Does David mean the grave, or a reunion after death? Jewish and Christian readers have heard both.
b: On the plainest reading, David means that he too will die and go down to the grave or to Sheol, the place of the dead, while the child cannot come back to life. Many Christian readers find more: a hope of being with the child after death, and this verse is often cited in teaching that infants who die are saved. Jewish commentators mostly read it as the grave and the end of mourning, though rabbinic tradition also holds that righteous children have a share in the world to come. The text itself does not settle the question. Either way, David's words are a turn from pleading to acceptance.

a: She named him Solomon
p: Solomon (Shelomoh) sounds like shalom, peace. Nathan adds a second name, Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD."
b: Shelomoh is related to shalom, "peace, wholeness," and 1 Chronicles 22:9 explains it as a sign of peace in his days. Some scholars suggest the name meant "his replacement" (from shillem, "to repay"), marking him as the child given in place of the one who died. "Jedidiah" (Yedidyah) means "beloved of the LORD"; yedid comes from the same root as "David" (dwd, "beloved"). The Hebrew text says "he called" (Ketiv) or "she called" (Qere); see the variant. Verse 12:25 does not say who gave the second name: most readers take it as the LORD, speaking through Nathan. The line "The LORD loved the boy" quietly points ahead to Solomon's kingship (1 Kings 1–2).

a: Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites
p: The story returns to the siege of 11:1. The events of chapters 11–12 happened during it.
b: The siege that began in 11:1 frames the whole Bathsheba story. Since the child of 11:27 was born and died, and Solomon was conceived, before the city fell, the siege may have lasted a year or two, or the writer may be finishing the war story out of strict time order. The "royal city" and the "water city" (12:27) are probably the lower town by the stream of the Jabbok's headwaters, which supplied the city's water. Once it fell, the citadel on the hill could not hold out long.

a: it will be called by my name
p: To have one's name "called over" a place meant to own it. Joab gives the honor of the conquest to David.
b: The idiom "my name will be called over it" means ownership, as when God's name is "called over" his people or his temple (Deuteronomy 28:10; Jeremiah 7:10). David had named his own conquest Jerusalem "the City of David" (5:9). Joab, loyal or calculating or both, makes sure the king gets the credit. He also gets David out of Jerusalem and back to the army, where a king belongs (11:1).

a: He took their king's crown off his head
p: A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg). Some think the crown belonged to the god Milcom's statue.
b: A talent of gold weighed roughly 34 kilograms (75 pounds), far too heavy to wear. Explanations: the crown was worn only briefly in a ceremony; the weight given is that of the whole treasure; or the crown sat on a statue of Milcom, the Ammonite god, whose name is spelled almost like "their king" (malkam; see the variant). The Talmud discusses how David could wear it at all and suggests a magnet held it above his head (Avodah Zarah 44a). The "precious stone" alone may have been placed on David's head.

a: set them at the saws, the iron picks and the iron axes
p: The KJV says David put the Ammonites "under saws" and through the brick kiln. Most now read it as forced labor.
b: The Hebrew says David "set" (wayyasem) the people "at" or "with" saws, picks and axes, and "made them pass" through the brick mold or brickworks. The KJV, following the older reading and 1 Chronicles 20:3 (which has wayyasar, "he sawed"), pictured torture: "put them under saws... and made them pass through the brickkiln." Most modern scholars think the tools are tools of work, and that David turned the captives into a labor force, as kings commonly did with conquered peoples (1 Kings 9:20–21). Some still hold the harsher reading. See the variant.

a: David's son Absalom had a sister, a beautiful girl named Tamar
p: Amnon was David's firstborn by Ahinoam. Absalom and Tamar were children of Maacah, a princess of Geshur.
b: The list of David's sons born at Hebron puts Amnon first, son of Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Absalom third, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (3:2–3). Tamar is Absalom's full sister and Amnon's half-sister. The narrator introduces her through Absalom, not through David, which signals who will act for her. The chapter is built to mirror chapter 11: a king's son sees a beautiful woman, uses a trick and a servant, and takes her, and a murder follows.

a: David's son Amnon loved her
p: The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for love. The story will show it was something else.
b: Hebrew ahav covers every kind of love, from Jacob's love for Rachel (Genesis 29:18) to Jonathan's for David (1 Samuel 18:1). The Mishnah uses this verse as its example of a love that "depends on a thing": "when the thing is gone, the love is gone," and it sets the love of Amnon for Tamar against the love of David and Jonathan, which did not depend on anything (Mishnah Avot 5:16). Modern readers often call Amnon's feeling obsession or lust; the narrator lets the word "love" stand and then shows it turn to hate in 13:15.

a: Because she was a virgin, doing anything to her looked impossible in Amnon's eyes
p: Unmarried princesses lived guarded lives. Amnon could not see Tamar alone without a plan.
b: Virgin daughters of the king wore a special robe (13:18) and lived in the women's quarters, where an unrelated man could not visit freely. Tamar's virginity also had value to the royal house in arranging a marriage. The verse admits plainly that Amnon was not thinking of marriage: what looked impossible was "to do anything to her." The words "in Amnon's eyes" recall that this whole story, like chapter 11, begins with looking (11:2; 13:5–6).

a: Jonadab was an extremely wise man
p: Hebrew chakham can mean skilled or shrewd as well as morally wise. Jonadab's wisdom serves evil.
b: Chakham describes the skilled craftsmen of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:6), the shrewd woman of Tekoa (14:2) and the wise woman of Abel (20:16). Jonadab's "wisdom" is cunning without conscience. He is David's nephew, son of Shimeah (called Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9), so he is Amnon's cousin. He reappears in 13:32–35, knowing more about Absalom's plans than anyone else, which makes some readers suspect he played both sides.

a: shape two heart-cakes while I watch
p: The Hebrew word for these cakes, levivot, sounds like lev, "heart." Amnon's request carries his desire in a pun.
b: The cakes (levivot) and the verb for making them (tilabbev) are both formed from lev or levav, "heart." They appear only in this chapter. They may have been heart-shaped, or a comforting food for the sick, or the word may simply be a pun the narrator enjoys: Amnon asks her to "heart" him some "hearts." The same verb in the Song of Songs means "you have stolen my heart" (Song of Songs 4:9). David hears only a sick son's request.

a: David sent a message to Tamar
p: As in chapter 11, David "sends," and a woman comes to a man's house. This time David is used by another.
b: In chapter 11 David sent for Bathsheba. Now, without knowing it, he sends his own daughter into Amnon's trap. Many readers see this as the start of the sword Nathan foretold (12:10): David's household repeats his own sin. David does not ask why Amnon wants Tamar in particular, which some read as innocence and others as a father's blindness that will show again in his handling of Amnon and Absalom.

a: Do not dishonor me
p: The verb 'innah means to humble or debase. It does not by itself say force; the context here does.
b: Hebrew 'innah (from 'anah, "be low") means to lower someone, to humble or shame. Used of a woman it means to have sex with her in a way that degrades her status, whether by force (Genesis 34:2; Judges 19:24; here) or without a proper marriage (Deuteronomy 22:29). This site renders it "dishonor" throughout. In this chapter the force is spelled out by the surrounding words: "he overpowered her" (13:14). Most modern versions translate the verb as "rape" or "violate" here, which is the meaning of the scene; the Plain English keeps the Hebrew word's own picture and lets 13:14 say the rest.

a: Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing.
p: Tamar uses the words of Genesis 34 and Judges 19: "a disgraceful thing" that is "not done" in Israel.
b: Tamar's protest is built from Israel's oldest moral vocabulary, and the Plain English renders her Hebrew idiom exactly as in Genesis. When Shechem took Dinah, her brothers were furious "because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing in Israel: he had lain with Jacob's daughter, and such a thing is not done" (Genesis 34:7). The old man of Gibeah pleaded, "do not do this disgraceful thing" (Judges 19:23), and the Levite later called the crime "a vile act, a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Judges 20:6). The word nevalah means a senseless, shameful act that breaks the community's basic decency. In each story the crime leads to a brother's or a tribe's revenge, and in each the violence spreads (Genesis 34:25–29; Judges 20).

a: you would be one of the disgraceful men in Israel
p: The word for these men, nevalim, shares its root with nevalah and with Nabal, the fool of 1 Samuel 25.
b: Tamar warns that Amnon would become one of the nevalim, people who do nevalah. The same root names Nabal, Abigail's husband, of whom she said, "Nabal is his name, and shameful folly is his companion" (1 Samuel 25:25). A naval in Hebrew is not someone with a low IQ but a person who acts as if there is no God and no moral order (Psalm 14:1). Tamar thinks of both of them, her shame and his.

a: He will not hold me back from you
p: The law forbids marriage to a half-sister. Tamar may be stalling, or the rule may not yet have been kept at court.
b: Leviticus forbids sex with "your sister, your father's daughter or your mother's daughter" (Leviticus 18:9; 20:17), and Deuteronomy curses it (Deuteronomy 27:22). Yet Abraham married his half-sister Sarah (Genesis 20:12). Readers explain Tamar's words in three ways: (1) she is buying time, saying anything to escape; (2) the laws were not yet observed, or not by the royal family, in David's day (many critical scholars); (3) the Talmud (Sanhedrin 21a) says Tamar's mother was a captive woman who conceived her before converting, so Tamar was not legally Amnon's sister. Whatever the case, Tamar offers a lawful path, and Amnon refuses it.
r: Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 18:11; Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 27:22; Genesis 20:12; Deuteronomy 21:10–14

a: He overpowered her, dishonored her and lay with her
p: The Hebrew says he "lay her," not "lay with her": a grammar of force, as with Dinah.
b: Three verbs follow quickly: he was stronger than her (wayyecheziq mimmennah), he dishonored her, he lay her. The last uses the object marker (et), "he lay her," instead of the usual "lay with her" ('im). The same unusual grammar appears in Genesis 34:2, where Shechem "took her and lay with her and dishonored her" (Genesis 34:2). Many scholars read the construction as stressing that she was the object of the act, not a partner. The verse also notes he "refused to listen to her voice": the narrator gives her a voice even if Amnon will not.

a: And now Amnon hated her, a huge hatred
p: The narrator stresses the reversal with four forms of "hate." Readers have long tried to explain it.
b: Hebrew repeats the word: he hated her a hatred, great; the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Rabbinic readers took this as proof that the love was never real (Mishnah Avot 5:16). One talmudic tradition says Amnon hated her because he was injured during the act (Sanhedrin 21a), a story many modern readers find troubling because it shifts attention to his body. Modern readers point to guilt turned outward: the one he wronged now reminds him of what he is. The narrator gives no reason, only the result.

a: This evil, throwing me out, is greater than the other one you have done to me
t: Why sending her away was worse
p: Under the law a man who violated a virgin had to marry her and could never divorce her.
b: Deuteronomy rules that a man who seizes an unpromised virgin and lies with her must pay her father and "she will become his wife, because he dishonored her. He may never send her away as long as he lives" (Deuteronomy 22:29). To a modern reader this sounds like a second injury, but in Tamar's world it was the only protection left to her: a woman who had lost her virginity could not expect another marriage, and would live without husband or children. By throwing her out, Amnon leaves her with shame and no future. The Hebrew of this verse is damaged (see the variant), but its sense is clear.

a: Throw this one out of here
p: Amnon will not even say her name or "woman." Hebrew has only zot, "this."
b: Hebrew shilchu-na et zot, "send away, please, this," uses only the feminine pronoun. English versions often add "woman." The contempt is in the missing noun. Earlier he called her "my sister" (13:11). He also has the servant bolt the door, which in the eyes of others would make it look as though she had come to him and been sent away, not the other way round.

a: a robe that reached to her hands and feet
t: The robe of Joseph and Tamar
p: The same rare phrase, ketonet passim, describes only Joseph's robe and Tamar's.
b: The phrase ketonet passim appears only here and in the Joseph story, where Jacob gave Joseph "a robe that reached to his hands and feet" (Genesis 37:3). The KJV's "coat of many colours" follows the Greek; the Hebrew probably means a long robe with sleeves to the wrists and hem to the ankles, a sign of status, not of work. Both robes are torn or stained after a brother's crime: Joseph's brothers dip his in blood (Genesis 37:31), and Tamar tears hers herself (13:19). Both stories also involve a brother who plots against a brother.

a: She laid her hand on her head and walked off, screaming as she went
p: Ashes, a torn garment, a hand on the head and loud cries were public signs of mourning and outrage.
b: Ashes on the head and torn clothes were standard signs of mourning (1:2; Joshua 7:6). A hand on the head seems to have meant shame or disaster (Jeremiah 2:37), a gesture also known from Egyptian art. Tamar does not hide what has happened. She goes out crying aloud, which under the law was evidence that a woman did not consent (Deuteronomy 22:24, 27). Her public protest is the opposite of the silence Absalom will ask of her in the next verse.

a: Was it Amnon your brother who was with you?
p: Absalom calls his brother by an odd form of his name, Aminon. Some hear contempt in it.
b: The Hebrew here spells the name Aminon, not Amnon. It may be a scribal slip, a nickname, or a deliberately belittling form ("little Amnon"), which would fit Absalom's hatred (13:22). The euphemism "was with you" is the kind of language a family uses to avoid saying what happened. Absalom seems to guess at once, which suggests he knew his brother.

a: For now, my sister, say nothing
p: Is Absalom protecting Tamar, or silencing her for his own plan? Readers disagree.
b: Absalom's words can sound like comfort: do not take it to heart; he is family. Many readers see them as protective, buying time and shielding her from more public shame. Others, especially feminist readers (Phyllis Trible), point out that his silence also silences her, and that he takes over her story for his own revenge and, later, his own ambitions. He even names his own daughter Tamar (14:27). Both readings can be true at once.

a: a woman left desolate
p: The Hebrew word shomemah is used of a ruined land or a woman with no husband or children.
b: Shomemah means desolate, abandoned, ruined: it describes cities laid waste (Isaiah 49:8) and the "desolate woman" who has no husband (Isaiah 54:1). It is the last word the Bible says about Tamar. She disappears from the story, and the next time her name is heard it belongs to Absalom's daughter (14:27). Many readers take the silence as part of the tragedy: the woman most wronged is the one whose future no one records.

a: it made him burn with rage
p: David is furious but does nothing. The longer text explains why: Amnon was his favorite and firstborn.
b: The law gave David, as king and father, the duty to act (Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 22:28–29). The Hebrew text says only that he was angry. The Greek and a Dead Sea scroll add that he did not want to hurt Amnon "because he loved him" (see the variant). Readers note that David's own crime may have tied his hands: how could he punish a son for what he had done himself? His failure to act leaves justice to Absalom, and so leads to murder. Some readers compare Eli, who heard of his sons' sins and did not restrain them (1 Samuel 3:13).

a: nothing bad and nothing good
p: A Hebrew idiom for "nothing at all." Laban was told the same about Jacob.
b: Hebrew lemera' we'ad tov, "from bad to good," pairs opposites to mean "anything at all," as when God warned Laban not to say anything to Jacob "good or bad" (Genesis 31:24, 29). Absalom's silence is not peace. For two years (13:23) he speaks no word, and his hatred grows behind it.

a: Absalom's sheep were being sheared
p: Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting and drinking, and in the Bible often of trouble.
b: Shearing time was a festival for sheep owners, with food and wine for workers and guests. Nabal held such a feast, and drunk at it, nearly brought death on his household (1 Samuel 25:2–11, 36). Judah was on his way to his shearers when he met his daughter-in-law Tamar at the roadside (Genesis 38:12–14), another Tamar wronged by a man of Judah's line. Absalom's invitation sounds natural, which is why it works. Baal-hazor is probably a high hill north of Bethel, about fifteen miles (25 km) from Jerusalem.

a: Am I not the one giving you the order?
p: Absalom, like David with Uriah, uses wine and servants to kill, and takes the blame on himself.
b: Readers have noted how Absalom repeats his father's crime against Uriah: a feast, wine to loosen a man (11:13), and a killing done by others at the order of a king's son. His words to his servants, "Be strong and act like brave men," echo the encouragement David sent to Joab after Uriah's death (11:25). Nathan's promise that disaster would rise "out of your own house" (12:11) is working itself out.

a: Each got on his mule, and they ran
p: Mules were the mounts of princes in David's court. Absalom will die riding one.
b: Horses were rare in Israel at this time, and mules, bred from horses and donkeys, seem to have been a mark of royalty: Solomon rides David's own mule to his anointing (1 Kings 1:33, 38). The law forbade breeding mixed animals (Leviticus 19:19), so mules were probably bought from abroad (1 Kings 10:25). The princes flee on them here, and Absalom will ride one to his death (18:9).

a: Absalom has had this planned, by his own word, since the day Amnon dishonored Tamar his sister
p: Jonadab, who advised Amnon, knew all along that Absalom planned to kill him.
b: The Hebrew phrase is unusual: "on the mouth of Absalom it was set," meaning Absalom had decided it, or perhaps that he had said so openly. Jonadab is calm while the king lies on the ground in grief, and he knows exactly who is dead. Some readers think he simply read Absalom well; others suspect he was a schemer who served whichever prince was rising. Either way, the friend who planned the rape now explains the murder.

a: Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur
p: Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee, ruled by Absalom's grandfather.
b: Talmai was the father of Absalom's mother Maacah (3:3), so Absalom fled to his grandfather. The last clause of 13:37 has no named subject in Hebrew; the Greek supplies "King David," and the Plain English follows that sense. Geshur lay in the Golan, north and east of the Sea of Galilee; excavations at et-Tell (often identified as Bethsaida) and Tel Hadar have uncovered fortified towns of this period that many link to the kingdom of Geshur. David's marriage to Maacah was probably a treaty marriage to secure his northern border (3:3). Absalom stays there three years.

a: The king's spirit pined to go out to Absalom
t: Longing for Absalom, or ceasing to march against him?
p: The Hebrew can mean David longed to go out to Absalom, or gave up going out against him. The oldest versions read "ceased."
b: The verb kalah means "to be finished, spent" or "to waste away" with longing, as in "My being yearns, and even wastes away" (Psalm 84:2). The oldest translations take the first sense: the Greek has ekopasen, "the king's spirit ceased, abated," and the Latin Vulgate has "King David ceased to pursue Absalom." The phrase latset 'el can mean "go out against," as an army does, and McCarter and others read: the king gave up marching out against Absalom. Medieval Jewish commentators, the KJV tradition and most modern versions read "longed to go out to Absalom," which the Plain English follows. The next verse (14:1) is two-sided in the same way. Joab's need to stage a drama, and David's refusal to see his son for two years (14:24, 28), suggest that his feelings were mixed at best.

a: the king's heart was turned toward Absalom
p: The Hebrew preposition 'al can mean "toward" or "against." Was David longing for Absalom or still angry?
b: Hebrew lev hammelekh 'al Avshalom is literally "the king's heart was on Absalom." With feelings, 'al often means "against" (Job 2:3), and some scholars read the verse that way: Joab saw that David was still set against his son and needed persuading. Most translations take it as longing, which fits 13:39 if that verse is read as longing; if 13:39 means that David "ceased" to march against Absalom, as the oldest versions read it, 14:1 may mean his heart was still set against him. The king's behavior after Absalom's return, refusing to see him for two years (14:24, 28), shows that whatever he felt, he did not fully forgive.

a: had a wise woman brought from there
p: Tekoa was a village south of Bethlehem, later home of the prophet Amos. "Wise women" may have had a public role.
b: Tekoa lay on the edge of the Judean wilderness, about ten miles (16 km) south of Jerusalem; Amos the prophet came from there (Amos 1:1). Two women in 2 Samuel are called "wise": this one and the woman of Abel who negotiates with Joab (20:16–22). Some scholars think wise women held a recognized public role as counselors or mediators, like Deborah "judging" Israel (Judges 4:4–5); others see them simply as clever individuals. Either way, the story credits a village woman with the skill to move a king, though the words were Joab's (14:3, 19).

a: And Joab put the words in her mouth
p: Joab writes the script but stays offstage. His motive is not given.
b: Joab "put the words in her mouth," the phrase used of God giving words to a prophet (Exodus 4:15; Jeremiah 1:9). The narrator does not say why Joab wants Absalom back. Possibilities: he cares for the king's grief; he sees Absalom as the likely heir and wants to be in his favor; or he fears the instability of an exiled prince with a foreign grandfather. Later Joab will kill this same Absalom against David's orders (18:14). The man who brought him home is the man who ends his life.

a: Save me, O king!
p: The woman cries hoshi'ah, "save!", the formal plea of someone asking the king for justice.
b: Hoshi'ah hammelekh is the cry of a subject asking the king to step in, as the starving woman cries to the king of Israel in 2 Kings 6:26. It uses the verb from which "Hosanna" ("save, please!") comes (Psalm 118:25; Mark 11:9). The king was the highest court in Israel, and anyone could appeal to him, which is exactly the role Absalom will later claim the king is failing to fill (15:2–4).

a: We will put him to death to pay for the life of the brother he killed
p: Israel's law let the nearest kinsman kill a murderer. Cities of refuge protected those who killed by accident.
b: In early Israel the "avenger of blood" (go'el haddam, 14:11), the dead man's nearest male kin, had the right to kill a murderer (Numbers 35:19). The law limited this: an accidental killer could flee to a city of refuge and stand trial (Numbers 35:12). The woman's case is built to be hard. Her son killed his brother in a fight, not by accident, so the avenger has the law on his side; but carrying it out would destroy the family the custom was meant to protect. Only the king can cut through the law, and that is the point Joab wants David to reach about his own son.
r: Numbers 35:12; Numbers 35:19–21; Deuteronomy 19:6; Deuteronomy 19:12; Genesis 9:6; Genesis 4:10–15

a: they would put out the one ember I have left
p: Her surviving son is the last live coal of a family fire. If he dies, her husband's name dies with him.
b: A household kept embers through the night to restart the fire; to lose the last one was to lose the hearth. The woman's image means that if her last son is executed, her husband's line ends. Ancient Israel cared deeply about a dead man's "name" continuing on his land, which is the concern behind the brother-in-law marriage of Deuteronomy 25:5–10 and the book of Ruth (Ruth 4:5, 10). The clan's demand for blood vengeance clashes with its own interest in keeping the family's land and name.

a: let any guilt fall on me and on my father's family
p: If the king lets a killer go, the guilt of unavenged blood might fall on the king. She offers to carry it.
b: Israel believed that innocent blood not answered for brought guilt on the land and its ruler (Numbers 35:33; Deuteronomy 21:1–9). By pardoning the son, the king would risk that guilt. The woman takes it on herself and her family. The king's promises grow step by step: first "I will give an order" (14:8), then protection (14:10), then an oath by the LORD (14:11). Once he has sworn, he is bound, and she can spring the trap.

a: the king does not bring home the one he banished
p: The woman says the king harms the whole nation by keeping the probable heir in exile.
b: Amnon, the firstborn, is dead, and David's second son Chileab (Daniel) is never mentioned again (3:3). Absalom is now the likely heir. A crown prince living abroad with a foreign king, his grandfather, was a danger to Israel's future. The woman's argument moves from her own case to the nation: if the king can spare her son for the family's sake, he should spare his own for the people's sake. Critics of David's choice point out that he applied the lesson to Absalom's banishment but never to Absalom's crime.

a: We are like water poured out on the ground, which no one can gather up
t: Water spilled, and a God who plans
p: A proverb about death leads to a claim: God does not just take life, but plans ways to bring the banished home.
b: The image of spilled water that cannot be gathered describes how final death is (Psalm 22:14). The rest of the verse is hard Hebrew. Read as the Plain English does, it says God "does not take a life away" but "works out plans" so the banished are not cast off for good. Jewish readers have taken it as a statement of God's mercy toward sinners. Many Christian readers see in it a picture of the gospel: God devising a way to bring home those cut off from him (2 Corinthians 5:18–19). Some scholars read the clause differently: "God will not take away the life of one who devises plans," urging the king to act. In context the woman's goal is plain: David should imitate God's mercy.

a: my lord the king is like God's angel at hearing out good and evil
p: Courtiers flatter David with this phrase three times. Each time, he is about to be deceived or to judge badly.
b: The woman uses the phrase twice (14:17, 20); the Philistine Achish used it of David (1 Samuel 29:9), and Mephibosheth will use it when David has to decide between his word and Ziba's (19:27). "Hearing out good and evil" means judging wisely between right and wrong, the gift Solomon asks for (1 Kings 3:9). The irony is that David is being skillfully managed even as he is praised for seeing through everything. He does guess Joab's hand (14:19), which shows he was not entirely fooled.

a: My face he will not see
p: Absalom returns to Jerusalem but is shut out of the court. Many read this half-measure as the seed of the revolt.
b: To "see the king's face" meant to be received at court, to be in favor (Genesis 43:3; Esther 1:14). David lets Absalom come home but keeps him away, for two full years (14:28). Readers have judged this in opposite ways: as a wise middle path between justice and mercy, or as the worst of both, neither punishing Absalom's murder nor restoring him as a son. The narrator repeats "the king's face he did not see" three times (14:24, 14:28) before Absalom forces a meeting.

a: From his heels to his scalp not a flaw could be found in him
p: The word for flaw, mum, is the word for a defect that kept an animal from being offered as a sacrifice.
b: Mum is used in the law for the blemishes that disqualified a sacrificial animal (Leviticus 22:20) or a priest (Leviticus 21:17). Absalom is described, physically, as a perfect offering. His good looks win the people (15:6), as Saul's height and David's handsome face once impressed Israel (1 Samuel 9:2; 1 Samuel 16:12). But the reader has heard that the LORD "sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The perfect outside will end hanging in a tree.

a: he would weigh his hair: two hundred shekels by the royal standard
p: Two hundred shekels is about five pounds. Later tradition tied his hair to his death, though 18:9 says his head.
b: A shekel weighed about 11.5 grams, so the hair weighed roughly 2.3 kilograms (five pounds), an exaggerated but vivid sign of vanity and vitality. The "royal standard" may have been a different weight from the common shekel. The Mishnah draws a moral: "Absalom gloried in his hair, therefore he was hanged by his hair" (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Popular retellings and paintings also show Absalom caught by his hair. The text in 18:9 says his "head caught fast in the oak," which may include his hair but does not say so. Some compare the Nazirite's uncut hair (Numbers 6:5) and Samson's (Judges 16:17), but Absalom cut his yearly.

a: Absalom had three sons born to him, and one daughter
p: Here Absalom has three sons, but in 18:18 he says he has no son. Readers have explained this in several ways.
b: Explanations: the sons died young, which is why they are not named (rabbinic commentators, and many modern ones); the monument of 18:18 was set up before they were born; or the two verses come from different sources (some critical scholars). Absalom names his daughter Tamar after his sister. The Greek adds that this Tamar became the wife of Rehoboam (see the variant); 1 Kings 15:2 names Rehoboam's wife as "Maacah daughter of Abishalom," which may mean Absalom's granddaughter through Tamar.

a: Go set fire to it
p: Absalom gets Joab's attention the way Samson got the Philistines': by burning their grain.
b: Burning a man's standing grain was a known act of provocation and revenge: Samson burned the Philistines' fields (Judges 15:4–5), and the law made anyone who started a field fire pay for it (Exodus 22:6). Absalom uses violence to get a meeting, which shows how he works. The report by Joab's servants, with their clothes torn, is found in a Hebrew scroll from Qumran (4QSam-c), in the Greek and in the Latin Vulgate, though not in the Leningrad Codex (see the variant).

a: And the king gave Absalom a kiss
p: The kiss ends the chapter. Was it real reconciliation or only a public gesture?
b: A kiss was a public sign of welcome and peace (Genesis 33:4; Luke 15:20). The narrator calls Absalom only "Absalom" here, never "his son," and records no words. Some readers see a genuine reunion, the father's heart winning out. Others notice that the next chapter begins at once with Absalom building his own support (15:1), and that Absalom himself will use kisses to steal hearts (15:5). Christian readers sometimes set the scene beside the parable of the lost son, where the father runs and kisses (Luke 15:20), and note the difference: there the son comes home in repentance, and the father calls him "my son."

a: a chariot and horses for himself, and fifty men who ran in front of him
p: A chariot, horses and runners were royal display. Adonijah will copy it exactly.
b: Samuel had warned that a king would take Israel's sons, and "they will run ahead of his chariot" (1 Samuel 8:11). Absalom puts on the trappings of kingship before he claims it. David himself seems to have used mules rather than chariot horses (13:29; 1 Kings 1:33). Years later Adonijah, David's next son, "got himself a chariot and horsemen, and fifty men running ahead of him" when he tried to seize the throne (1 Kings 1:5). In both cases David does nothing to stop it.

a: taking his stand by the road leading to the gate
p: The city gate was the courtroom of ancient Israel. Absalom stands where plaintiffs pass on their way to the king.
b: Elders heard cases in the gate (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–11), and gate complexes excavated at sites like Dan and Gezer have benches where such business was done. Cases that local elders could not settle went to the king. Absalom catches people before they reach David, and asks first where they are from. His questions single out northerners ("one of Israel's tribes"), which hints at the tension between Israel and Judah that runs through the book and breaks out again in chapters 19–20.

a: But the king has no one to listen to you
t: Was David failing as a judge?
p: Absalom claims the king neglects justice. The story does not say whether that was true.
b: Earlier the narrator praised David for doing justice for all his people (8:15). Absalom says otherwise, and his campaign works, which suggests there were real grievances, perhaps especially in the north. Some historians think David's growing administration, with its officials and forced labor (20:24), had made the king remote. Others take Absalom's words as pure manipulation: he tells every man his case is good before hearing the other side. Proverbs warns that the first to plead seems right until the other comes and questions him (Proverbs 18:17).

a: And so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel
p: In English, stealing hearts sounds like winning love. In Hebrew, "stealing the heart" means deceiving.
b: The Hebrew idiom ganav lev means to deceive someone, to go behind his back. Jacob "stole the heart of Laban" when he left without telling him (Genesis 31:20, 26). So the verse says more than that Absalom became popular: it says he won the people by fooling them. The Plain English keeps the image because the Hebrew repeats it; this note gives its meaning. The rabbis said Absalom stole three hearts, his father's, the court's and Israel's, and so three sticks pierced his heart (Mishnah Sotah 1:8; 18:14).

a: pay my vow, the one I vowed to the LORD, in Hebron
p: Hebron was Absalom's birthplace and David's first capital. Judah's old center may have resented Jerusalem.
b: David reigned in Hebron for seven and a half years before moving to Jerusalem (5:5), and Absalom was born there (3:2–3). Moving the capital to Jerusalem may have left Hebron's leaders feeling pushed aside. A vow made in exile (15:8) gave Absalom a religious reason to go, the same cover Samuel once used when he went to Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:2). Hebron was also where Abraham was buried and where David had first been anointed king of Judah (2:4).

a: I made a vow
p: A vow promised God a gift or act of worship if he granted a request. It was a serious obligation.
b: Israelites often made conditional vows: if God does this, I will do that (Genesis 28:20–22; 1 Samuel 1:11). Keeping a vow was required (Deuteronomy 23:21–23). Absalom's request is therefore hard for David to refuse without seeming to stand between his son and God. "Serve the LORD" here probably means offering sacrifices (15:12). Whether Absalom ever made the vow, the narrator leaves us to judge.

a: Absalom is king in Hebron!
p: A blast on the ram's horn and the shout "X is king!" made a king in ancient Israel.
b: The same pattern marks Solomon's coronation: the horn is blown and the people shout, "Long live King Solomon!" (1 Kings 1:34, 39), and Jehu's: "Jehu is king!" (2 Kings 9:13). The Psalms use the cry of God: "The LORD is king" (Psalm 93:1). Absalom plans a signal that will carry from town to town across the tribes, so that the revolt appears everywhere at once.

a: Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's adviser
p: David's most trusted counselor joins the revolt. He may have been Bathsheba's grandfather.
b: Ahithophel came from Giloh, a town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:51). His advice was treated like a word from God (16:23). His son Eliam is listed among David's Thirty (23:34). If that Eliam is Bathsheba's father (11:3), Ahithophel was her grandfather, a family tree the Talmud assumes (Sanhedrin 69b). The Talmud gives his motive as ambition: he misread signs that kingship would come from him, when it was to come through Bathsheba (Sanhedrin 101b). Many modern commentators suggest revenge for Bathsheba instead, and point to his advice that Absalom publicly take David's concubines (16:21) as repaying David in kind. The text itself never states a motive.

a: Up! Let's run
p: David leaves his fortified capital without a fight. Readers give strategic, moral and spiritual reasons.
b: Strategic: Jerusalem could not hold out against a revolt that had all Israel behind it, and David needed time to gather loyal forces east of the Jordan, where he could choose the ground (17:8–14). Moral: he says he wants to spare the city from the sword (15:14). Spiritual: he accepts the disaster as from God (15:25–26; 16:10–12), the outworking of Nathan's word (12:10–11). The heading of Psalm 3 ties that psalm to this flight: "A psalm of David, when he ran away from his son Absalom" (Psalm 3:0).

a: He left ten women, concubines, to look after the house
p: Concubines were secondary wives. Leaving them behind sets up the fulfillment of Nathan's word in 16:22.
b: A concubine (pilegesh) was a wife of lower status, often without a dowry; her children could still be heirs. David leaves ten to keep the palace. The reader who remembers 12:11 knows what will happen. After the revolt David shuts them up "like widows" for the rest of their lives (20:3), a quiet note about women who paid for the sins of the men around them.

a: All the Kerethites and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites
p: David's most loyal troops were foreigners: Cretans, Philistines and six hundred men from Gath.
b: The Kerethites and Pelethites were David's personal bodyguard under Benaiah (8:18; 20:23). The names probably mean Cretans and Philistines, peoples of Aegean origin (1 Samuel 30:14; Ezekiel 25:16). The Gittites are men of Gath, the Philistine city where David once served Achish (1 Samuel 27). Kings often trusted foreign guards, who had no local family ties and depended on the king alone. As in chapter 11 with Uriah, outsiders prove more loyal than Israelites.

a: You are a foreigner, and an exile from your own place besides
p: Ittai is a nokhri, a man from another nation, the word Ruth used of herself.
b: Hebrew nokhri is a person from another people, as Ruth calls herself "a foreigner" (Ruth 2:10). David tells Ittai that he owes nothing to this quarrel and even calls Absalom "the king." Ittai had arrived only "yesterday," and David does not want to drag a refugee into another exile. His reply in 15:21 shows that loyalty is not a matter of birth.

a: Loyal love and faithfulness be with you
p: David blesses Ittai with the pair hesed and emet, the words God used to describe himself at Sinai.
b: Hesed we'emet, "loyal love and faithfulness," is the pair used when God passes before Moses, "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6), and in many blessings and psalms (2:6; Psalm 25:10). David has nothing to give Ittai but a wish that God will be loyal to him. The Greek adds "and may the LORD show you" (see the variant), which makes the sense explicit. The irony is that Ittai answers by showing hesed himself.

a: in whatever place my lord the king is, for death or for life, your servant will be right there
p: A foreign soldier's pledge echoes the foreign woman Ruth's: where you go, I will go.
b: Ruth the Moabite told Naomi: "where you go, I will go, and where you spend the night, I will spend the night" (Ruth 1:16), and "Where you die, I will die" (Ruth 1:17). Ittai the Philistine says the same to David, Ruth's great-grandson, and seals it with an oath by the LORD. In both stories a foreigner chooses loyalty to Israel's God and Israel's family when going home would have been easier. Christian readers have heard an echo too in Peter's promise to follow Jesus to death (Luke 22:33).

a: The king was crossing the Kidron Valley
t: Across the Kidron, up the Mount of Olives
p: David's route, across the Kidron and up the Mount of Olives in tears, is the route Jesus took on his last night.
b: The Kidron is the valley on the east side of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives. John notes that Jesus, betrayed by a friend who ate at his table, "went out across the Kidron Valley" to the garden (John 18:1), and the Gospels place his agony and arrest on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). Many Christian readers, from the church fathers on, have read David's flight as a foreshadowing: the rejected king, betrayed by his trusted counselor, weeping on the same slope. Jewish readers see in it David's humility under God's discipline.

a: and Abiathar went up
p: The Hebrew says only that Abiathar "went up." Many translations read it as "offered sacrifices."
b: Hebrew wayya'al Evyatar means "and Abiathar went up." The causative form of the same verb (he'elah) is used for offering a burnt offering, and some translations take the verse that way, as if the text meant that Abiathar offered sacrifices while the people passed. Others read that Abiathar "came up" to join Zadok, or went up the slope. The Plain English keeps the plain sense. It is also odd that Abiathar appears without the Levites who carry the ark, and that he is named after Zadok's group has already set it down; some scholars think the verse has been rearranged or expanded, perhaps to give Zadok, the later chief priest, the main role (1 Kings 2:26–27, 35).

a: Take God's ark back into the city
p: David refuses to carry the ark as a good-luck charm. He leaves his future to God.
b: A generation earlier Israel carried the ark into battle as if it would guarantee victory, and lost both the battle and the ark (1 Samuel 4:3–11). David will not use God's presence as a tool. He says the LORD will bring him back if he finds favor, and if not, "here I am. Let him do with me whatever looks good to him" (15:26), words like Eli's when he heard God's judgment: "Let him do whatever looks good to him" (1 Samuel 3:18). Practically, the ark and the priests in Jerusalem also give David friends inside Absalom's capital (15:27–28).

a: David was climbing the slope of the Olives, crying as he climbed
p: A covered head and bare feet were signs of mourning and shame, the same signs the prophets used.
b: Covering the head was a gesture of grief or disgrace (Jeremiah 14:3–4; Esther 6:12), and going barefoot was a sign of mourning or captivity (Isaiah 20:2–4; Ezekiel 24:17). David goes up the Mount of Olives as a mourner, and all the people mourn with him. Psalm 3, whose heading sets it in this flight, turns from "how many are my enemies" to trust in the LORD who answers "from his holy mountain" (Psalm 3:4), the mountain David is leaving.
r: Jeremiah 14:3–4; Esther 6:12; Isaiah 20:2–4; Ezekiel 24:17; Psalm 3:1–4; Zechariah 14:4

a: LORD, please make Ahithophel's advice foolish
p: David prays one sentence. In the next verse, Hushai appears at the top of the hill.
b: David asks God to turn Ahithophel's advice into folly (sakkel, "make foolish"). The answer comes as he reaches the summit: Hushai is waiting (15:32), and David at once sees how to use him. The narrator later states plainly that the LORD had ordained the defeat of Ahithophel's good advice (17:14). The story shows a theme common in Samuel: God works through human planning, loyalty and even trickery, not only through miracles. Jewish and Christian readers both point to the pattern of prayer joined with action.

a: where people bowed down to God
t: A place of worship on the summit
p: There seems to have been a shrine on top of the Mount of Olives where travelers worshiped.
b: The Hebrew says David came to the top "where one bows down to God," which suggests a known place of prayer. Before the temple, Israelites worshiped at hilltop shrines, "high places," which were not yet forbidden (1 Kings 3:2–4). Later Solomon built shrines to foreign gods on the hill east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), the same ridge. Here it is the place where David, at his lowest, bows to God before going on.

a: Hushai, David's friend
p: "Friend of the king" was probably a court title, like a personal adviser.
b: Hushai is called "David's friend" here and in 16:16, and 1 Kings 4:5 lists "the king's friend" among Solomon's officials. Similar titles are known in Egypt. The title adds weight to Absalom's sneer, "Is this your loyal love for your friend?" (16:17). Hushai was an Arkite, from a clan on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin (Joshua 16:2), so he too may have been of non-Israelite descent.

a: Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, came to meet him
p: Ziba brings gifts and an accusation. Later Mephibosheth will tell a very different story.
b: Ziba was Saul's steward, whom David had put in charge of Mephibosheth's lands (9:9–10). He arrives with exactly what a fleeing army needs, and with a charge that his master hopes to regain Saul's throne. When David returns, Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him and left him behind, since he was lame and could not saddle his own donkey (19:24–30). Most readers find Mephibosheth's account more believable: a disabled grandson of Saul had little hope of being made king by Absalom's rebels. Others think the narrator deliberately leaves the truth open, as David himself does in 19:29. Either way, a well-timed gift buys Ziba an estate.

a: the wine is drink for anyone worn out in the wilderness
t: Food for a king in flight
p: Like Abigail before him, Ziba meets David's need with bread, raisins, fruit and wine.
b: Abigail brought David "two hundred loaves, two skins of wine" (1 Samuel 25:18), along with raisins and fig cakes, when he was an outlaw. Ziba's gift is similar, and so is its purpose: to win the favor of a powerful man at a turning point. In 17:27–29 three more friends will bring supplies to David in Mahanaim. The narrator notes each act of kindness in David's worst days, and David remembers them when he returns (19:31–39).

a: where is your master's son?
p: Mephibosheth was Saul's grandson. Hebrew "son" often means any male descendant.
b: Mephibosheth was the son of Jonathan and the grandson of Saul (4:4; 9:6). Ziba's "master" is Saul, so "your master's son" means Saul's descendant, as "son" in Hebrew commonly includes grandsons (Genesis 29:5, where Laban, Nahor's grandson, is called his son). Mephibosheth's supposed hope that "the house of Israel will hand my father's kingdom back to me" means Saul's kingdom.

a: named Shimei son of Gera
p: Shimei is a Benjaminite of Saul's clan. His curses show how many in Benjamin still saw David as a usurper.
b: Bahurim lay just east of the Mount of Olives, on the road to the Jordan; Michal's husband Paltiel had followed her weeping as far as Bahurim (3:16). Shimei belongs to the same clan as Saul's family, and his outburst shows that resentment over the fall of Saul's house was alive a generation later. David will spare him twice (16:11; 19:23), but on his deathbed tells Solomon to deal with him (1 Kings 2:8–9, 36–46).

a: you man stained with blood
p: Shimei blames David for the blood of Saul's house. The book has insisted David was innocent of it.
b: Shimei calls David "a man of blood" and says the LORD has paid him back "all the blood of Saul's family" (16:8). The books of Samuel go out of their way to show David innocent of the deaths of Saul (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 1), Abner (3:28–39) and Ish-bosheth (4:9–12). Shimei may have had these in mind, or the execution of Saul's seven descendants told in 21:1–14 (which may have happened earlier than its place in the book). Critical historians (Halpern, McKenzie) think Shimei voices what many really believed, and that the book was written partly to answer such charges. The reader, who knows about Uriah, can see that David is a man of blood, just not of the blood Shimei names.

a: Why let this dead dog curse my lord the king?
p: Calling someone a "dead dog" made him worthless. David once used it of himself.
b: Dogs in Israel were scavengers, not pets, and a dead dog was the lowest thing imaginable. David used it of himself before Saul (1 Samuel 24:14), and Mephibosheth of himself before David (9:8). Abishai, Joab's brother, is quick to kill: he wanted to spear Saul in his sleep (1 Samuel 26:8). David restrains him both times.

a: What do you and I have in common, you sons of Zeruiah?
p: A Hebrew idiom for "this is none of your business" or "we see this differently." Jesus uses it to his mother.
b: Hebrew mah li walakhem is literally "what to me and to you?" It distances the speaker from the other person's view, sometimes sharply (Judges 11:12; 1 Kings 17:18). The same expression, in Greek, is Jesus' answer to his mother at Cana (John 2:4). David uses it again of Abishai's eagerness to kill Shimei (19:22). The "sons of Zeruiah" (Joab and Abishai, David's nephews) stand for violence that David cannot or will not control (3:39).

a: He curses this way because the LORD told him, 'Curse David.'
p: David treats the curse as coming from God, while Shimei remains responsible. Readers weigh how both can be true.
b: David does not say Shimei is right; he says he cannot rule out that God is behind the curse, and so he accepts it as discipline. This fits the Bible's broad view that God can use even hostile people for his purposes (Genesis 50:20; Isaiah 10:5–7) without excusing them: Shimei is later punished (1 Kings 2:44). Jewish commentators (Radak) read David's words as humility under judgment. Christian readers have compared Jesus, who did not answer insults with insults (1 Peter 2:23). David's "Maybe" in 16:12 is honest: he hopes but does not presume.

a: my son, who came from my own body, is out to take my life
p: "Who came from my body" echoes the promise of 7:12, where an heir from David's own body would build God's house.
b: In Nathan's promise God told David he would raise up an heir who would come from David's own body and would establish his kingdom (7:12). Here David uses nearly the same words for the son seeking his life. The contrast shows how far things have fallen since chapter 7, and why the question of who will succeed David drives the rest of the book (1 Kings 1). David's reasoning is a "how much more" argument (Hebrew qal wachomer), a form the rabbis later used often.

a: came in worn out, and there he caught his breath
t: Worn out, or a place called Ayephim?
p: The Hebrew word for "worn out" may be a place name. The verse seems to need one after "there."
b: The verse says the king came 'ayefim, "weary," and "refreshed himself there," but never says where "there" is. Some scholars think 'Ayefim was a place on the road to the Jordan. Some Greek manuscripts (the Lucianic text) add "to the Jordan," supplying the missing place. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew word in its ordinary sense. Either way, David and his people pause in exhaustion, and in 17:22 they cross the river.

a: "Long live the king!" Hushai said to Absalom. "Long live the king!"
p: Hushai never names the king he hails. Every word he says to Absalom can be heard two ways.
b: "Long live the king" was the shout at a coronation (1 Samuel 10:24; 1 Kings 1:25, 39). Hushai says it twice and does not say "King Absalom." In 16:18 he pledges himself to "the one the LORD has chosen," which Absalom hears as himself and the reader hears as David. In 16:19 he says he will serve "before" Absalom as he served before his father. Readers enjoy the double meanings as a contest of loyalty fought with words.

a: Is this your loyal love for your friend?
p: Absalom uses hesed, the loyalty owed in a covenant bond. He is mocking, but the word fits Hushai better than he knows.
b: Hebrew hesed is loyal love, the faithfulness owed within a relationship (Genesis 21:23; 1 Samuel 20:14–15). Absalom taunts Hushai for deserting his "friend." In fact Hushai is showing exactly that loyalty, by staying behind as David's spy. The scene is full of irony: the son who betrayed his father mocks a friend for betrayal.

a: Go in to your father's concubines
t: A public claim to the throne
p: Taking the king's women declared that the old king was finished. It also made reconciliation impossible.
