b: Ahithophel's advice had two goals. Taking the royal women was a claim to the throne (see 12:8; 1 Kings 2:22). It also made the break with David final: once Absalom had done this, his followers knew there could be no deal in which they would be abandoned ("everyone on your side will grow bolder"). Reuben's act with his father's concubine cost him his firstborn's place (Genesis 35:22; Genesis 49:4). The phrase "made yourself stink" (niv'ashta) is used of Israel becoming hateful to the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:4).

a: So they set up the tent for Absalom on the roof
p: Nathan's word in 12:11 comes true on the roof where David first saw Bathsheba.
b: Nathan had said: "I will take your wives while you watch and give them to someone close to you. He will sleep with your wives with this very sun watching" (12:11). Here it happens "with all Israel watching," on the roof of the king's house, where the story of David's sin began (11:2). "The tent" may be a wedding tent or canopy, like the one in Psalm 19:5. The narrator does not comment; the echo is the comment.

a: as if someone had asked for a word from God
p: To "ask for a word from God" meant consulting him through a priest or prophet. Ahithophel's advice had that weight.
b: Israelites "asked" God (sha'al) through the priest's ephod and the Urim and Thummim (1 Samuel 23:9–12; 30:7–8), or through a prophet (1 Kings 22:5). David did so often (2:1; 5:19). Saying that Ahithophel's advice was like a divine answer is high praise. It also sets up the drama of chapter 17: when Hushai defeats Ahithophel's advice, the narrator explains that it was God's doing (17:14). The best human counsel cannot stand against the LORD.

a: I will set out and chase after David this very night
p: Strike fast, while David is tired, and kill only the king. Most military readers judge it the winning plan.
b: Ahithophel's advice is simple: a picked force, a night pursuit, panic in David's camp, and one death. It would have avoided a civil war and handed Absalom the whole nation. Commentators of every school agree that it was good advice; the narrator calls it that (17:14). Its weakness, from Absalom's point of view, is that it gives the glory and the command to Ahithophel ("let me choose... I will set out... I will strike"). Hushai plays on exactly that.

a: the way a bride comes back to her husband
p: Ahithophel pictures the nation coming back to Absalom like a bride to her husband, once David is dead.
b: This image comes from the Greek text; the Hebrew is garbled here (see the variant). The picture is of a people whose loyalty is pledged to the king as a bride is pledged to a husband. The prophets use the same marriage language for Israel and the LORD (Hosea 2:16–20; Jeremiah 2:2). Coming from the man who has just advised Absalom to take his father's wives, the image is chilling: the kingdom too is a bride to be taken.

a: This time the advice Ahithophel has given is not good
p: Hushai's opening is tactful: Ahithophel's advice is usually good, but not this time.
b: Hushai cannot simply attack the most respected counselor in the land (16:23). By saying "this time," he grants Ahithophel's reputation and makes his own objection sound careful. His speech that follows is long, full of vivid pictures and flattery, in contrast to Ahithophel's short, practical plan. Literary readers note how the narrator gives Hushai more words and better images, so that the reader too is half-persuaded.

a: like a bear in the open country whose cubs have been taken
t: A bear robbed of her cubs
p: A she-bear who has lost her cubs was the Bible's picture of the most dangerous animal there is.
b: Syrian brown bears lived in Israel's hills until modern times. "Meet a mother bear robbed of her cubs, / but do not meet a fool in his folly" (Proverbs 17:12), and God threatens to meet faithless Israel "like a bear robbed of her cubs" (Hosea 13:8). Hushai paints David's men as "angry to the bone" (literally "bitter of soul") and David as an old fighter who will not be caught sleeping among his troops, as Saul once was (1 Samuel 26:7).

a: from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand beside the sea
p: Hushai's plan sounds grander but needs time to gather the whole nation. Time is what David needs.
b: "From Dan to Beersheba" means the whole land, north to south (Judges 20:1; 1 Samuel 3:20). "As many as the sand beside the sea" recalls the promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Hushai offers Absalom a vision of himself leading all Israel in person, the kind of glory Ahithophel's plan withheld. The practical effect is delay: calling out the whole nation would take days, while David crossed the Jordan and organized his veterans (17:22).

a: settle on him the way dew settles on the ground
p: Dew covers every inch of ground silently. Hushai pictures an army so large nothing could escape it.
b: Dew is usually a picture of blessing in the Bible (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5), and of quiet, total coverage (Judges 6:37–40). Hushai uses it for an army spreading over every hiding place. Together with the pictures of the bear (17:8), the lion (17:10), the sand (17:11) and the town hauled down with ropes (17:13), it makes his speech far more vivid than Ahithophel's.

a: The LORD had given orders to undo Ahithophel's good advice
p: One of the few places in chapters 9–20 where the narrator says plainly what God was doing.
b: Gerhard von Rad pointed out that the story of David's court almost never shows God acting openly: no miracles, few prophets. Instead, three short statements reveal God's hand: the LORD's displeasure (11:27), the LORD's love for Solomon (12:24), and this verse. Human beings make their plans, and God steers through them, answering David's prayer of 15:31. Jewish and Christian readers have used the verse as a key text on providence. Critical scholars debate whether such verses were part of the original court story or were added by a theological editor.

a: Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel
p: En-rogel was a spring outside Jerusalem. A slave girl carried messages so the priests' sons stayed unseen.
b: En-rogel was a spring in the Kidron Valley south of the city, on the border of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:7). Adonijah later held his feast there (1 Kings 1:9). The chain was Hushai to the priests, the priests to a slave girl going to the spring as if to draw water, and the girl to their sons, who ran to David. It is one of the few ancient stories to show such an intelligence network in detail.

a: His wife took the cover, stretched it over the opening of the well
p: Like Rahab and Michal, a woman saves the spies by hiding them and misleading the searchers.
b: Rahab hid Joshua's spies under flax on her roof and sent the searchers off on a false trail (Joshua 2:4–7). Michal let David down through a window and put an idol in his bed (1 Samuel 19:11–17). The woman of Bahurim covers a well with grain spread to dry and tells Absalom's men the messengers have gone on. The Bible reports these deceptions without condemning them, and many Jewish and Christian ethicists have read them as justified to save life; others hold that lying is never right, and see these women as praised for their courage, not for their words.

a: They went on across the water channel
p: The Hebrew word for "water channel" appears only here. Its meaning is a guess from context.
b: Hebrew mikhal hammayim appears nowhere else. Proposed meanings include "stream," "brook," "reservoir" or "channel"; the Greek translators seem not to have known it either. Some scholars connect it to a root meaning "to contain." The Plain English gives a general meaning. The point is simply that the woman sends the searchers further down the road, toward the Jordan.

a: He gave orders for his household, then hanged himself
p: Ahithophel saw that the revolt was lost. He is one of the few in the Bible who hang themselves; Judas is another.
b: Ahithophel goes home and puts his affairs in order, a phrase used of a dying man (2 Kings 20:1). Readers agree he foresaw that with his advice rejected, Absalom would lose, and that he himself, the chief traitor, would be executed. He is buried in his father's tomb, unlike Saul, whose body was first hung on the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10), which suggests his death brought no public dishonor on his body. Christian readers from early times linked him with Judas, the friend who betrayed his master and then hanged himself (Matthew 27:5), especially through Psalm 41:9, which Jesus applies to Judas in John 13:18 in a shorter form: "The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me." The Mishnah lists Ahithophel among those who have no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2).
r: 2 Kings 20:1; Matthew 27:3–5; Psalm 41:9; John 13:18; Psalm 55:12–14; Acts 1:16–18

a: By then David had reached Mahanaim
p: Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, had been the capital of Saul's son Ish-bosheth. It became David's base.
b: Mahanaim ("two camps") was where Jacob met God's angels (Genesis 32:2) and where Abner set up Ish-bosheth as king (2:8). It lay in Gilead, probably near the Jabbok River. Its location east of the Jordan gave David a defensible base among people loyal to him, with the river between him and Absalom. The site has not been identified with certainty; Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi is a common proposal.

a: Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite
p: Absalom's general was David's nephew and Joab's cousin. The family tree has puzzles.
b: Amasa's mother Abigail (spelled Abigal here) was the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. 1 Chronicles 2:16–17 lists Zeruiah and Abigail as daughters of Jesse, David's sisters, and calls Amasa's father "Jether the Ishmaelite." Here Abigail is "Nahash's daughter." Explanations: Nahash was the name of their mother, or of a first husband of Jesse's wife, making them David's half-sisters; or "Nahash" slipped in from 17:27. "Israelite" for Ithra is odd, since everyone in the story is Israelite, so Chronicles' "Ishmaelite" may be the better reading (see the variant). The civil war is a family war: Joab and Amasa, cousins, command the two armies, and Joab will later murder Amasa (20:8–10).

a: Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
t: Three friends east of the Jordan
p: An Ammonite prince, Mephibosheth's former host and a rich old Gileadite feed David's army.
b: Shobi was a son of Nahash, the Ammonite king whose kindness David had wanted to repay (10:2), and brother of Hanun, who insulted David's envoys. After Rabbah fell (12:29), Shobi may have ruled Ammon under David. Machir of Lo-debar had sheltered Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, before David took him in (9:4–5). Barzillai was a wealthy old man of Gilead whom David will reward (19:31–39; 1 Kings 2:7). Former enemies and former followers of Saul's house now stand by David, a sign of how his kindness in better days is repaid.

a: lentils, roasted grain,
p: The Hebrew lists "roasted grain" twice. The second is probably a copying slip, or a different kind of roasted food.
b: The list ends with qali, "roasted grain," a second time. Most scholars think a scribe copied the word twice by mistake; some suggest the second refers to roasted seeds or pulses. The Plain English keeps both, as the Hebrew has them. The long list itself, beds, bowls, pots, grain, beans, honey and cheese, shows how much the friends gave.

a: one third under Joab's command, one third under Abishai
p: Dividing an army into three was a standard tactic. One of the three commanders is a foreigner.
b: Gideon (Judges 7:16), Saul (1 Samuel 11:11) and the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:17) all used three divisions. David trusts Ittai the Gittite, who had joined him only days before (15:19–22), with a third of his army, equal to his nephews Joab and Abishai. The arrangement may also have been meant to balance Joab's power, which David could not otherwise check (3:39).

a: But you are like ten thousand of us
p: The army knew the enemy wanted only David. A king who stayed safe meant the war could not be lost in one blow.
b: Ahithophel had said exactly this: kill the king alone and the war is over (17:2). The troops see it too. Their words also show love for David. In 21:17, after David nearly dies in battle, his men swear he must never go out with them again, "so that you do not put out the lamp of Israel." The scene reverses 11:1, where David stayed in Jerusalem while others fought, and with tragic results. This time staying behind is wise, and the result is tragic all the same.

a: Go easy, for my sake, on the young man, on Absalom
p: David calls Absalom "the young man" five times in this chapter, as though he were still a boy.
b: Hebrew na'ar means a boy, a youth or a young servant. Absalom is a grown man with children (14:27), leading a rebellion. Yet David speaks of him as "the young man" (18:5, 12, 29, 32), the word a father might use of a son who has gone wrong. The order to go "easy" (le'at, "gently, slowly") is heard by the whole army (18:5, 12), which makes Joab's disobedience a public act.

a: the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim
t: A forest of Ephraim east of the Jordan?
p: Ephraim's land lay west of the Jordan, but the battle seems to be in Gilead, near Mahanaim.
b: The battle takes place near Mahanaim, east of the Jordan (17:24–26; 18:3), yet the forest is named for Ephraim, a tribe west of the river. Explanations: Ephraimites had settled or claimed land in Gilead (Judges 12:4 may hint at this); the forest got its name from some event in Ephraim's history; or the name refers to a wooded region west of the river after all. Gilead was known for its thick forests and rough ground (Jeremiah 22:6), which explains how "the forest ate up" more men than the sword (18:8).

a: the forest ate up more of the army that day than the sword ate
p: Ravines, thickets and pits killed more of Absalom's men than David's soldiers did.
b: Hebrew uses the same verb, "ate," for both the forest and the sword. In a wooded, broken landscape, a large army like Absalom's levy of "all Israel" (17:11) lost its advantage of numbers; fleeing men fell into ravines and pits, like the one Absalom is thrown into (18:17). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see God's hand in the terrain, as the narrator has said God was against Absalom (17:14). Others read it simply as the advantage of David's seasoned troops in rough country.

a: His head caught fast in the oak
p: Paintings show Absalom hanging by his long hair. The text says his head caught in the oak.
b: The popular picture comes from linking 14:26 (his heavy hair) with this verse, and the Mishnah already says "he was hanged by his hair" (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Josephus says the same (Antiquities 7.10.2). The Hebrew says wayyecheziq rosho ba'elah, "his head held fast in the oak," perhaps wedged in a fork of the branches. His hair may have been tangled too, but the text does not mention it. Either way, his famous beauty (14:25–26) becomes his trap.

a: he was left between the sky and the ground while the mule beneath him went on
p: The royal mule leaves its rider hanging. Many readers see the kingdom walking out from under Absalom.
b: Mules were the mounts of David's sons and of the king himself (13:29; 1 Kings 1:33). As the mule walks on, Absalom is left suspended, belonging neither to heaven nor to earth. The Hebrew verb is simply "he was put" (wayyuttan); the Greek has "he was hung." Many readers, ancient and modern, take this as a picture of his lost claim to the throne. The law says that a man "hanged on a tree" is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul applies that verse to Christ (Galatians 3:13); some Christian readers draw a contrast between the son who hung on a tree for his own rebellion and the Son who hung there for others.

a: Even if I could feel a thousand pieces of silver weighed into my palms
p: An unnamed soldier refuses a bribe and tells Joab to his face that Joab would have abandoned him.
b: The soldier understands court politics better than his commander expects. He heard the king's order, he knows nothing stays hidden from the king (as the woman of Tekoa found, 14:19–20), and he knows Joab would not have protected him (18:13). His refusal recalls David's own refusal to lift his hand against Saul, "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9). The narrator gives him more words than Joab, and a better conscience.

a: He took three sticks in his hand and drove them into Absalom's heart
p: The Hebrew word shevatim usually means staffs or rods, not spears. The "heart" of the oak echoes the heart of Absalom.
b: Shevatim are usually rods, clubs or staffs; translations vary between "darts," "javelins" and "spears." They may have been sharpened sticks, or Joab may have beaten him. "Heart" (lev) is used twice: Absalom's heart and "the heart of the oak," its middle. Absalom, who "stole the hearts" of Israel (15:6), is struck in the heart. The Mishnah turns this into a lesson: because he stole three hearts, three sticks pierced him (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Joab acts in open defiance of the king, as he did when he killed Abner (3:27).

a: ten young men, Joab's armor bearers
p: Joab's ten armor bearers finish Absalom off, making the killing a shared act.
b: Great warriors had armor bearers who carried their weapons and finished off the wounded (1 Samuel 14:13). By having ten men strike Absalom, Joab spreads the responsibility and makes sure the job is done. The Mishnah connects the number with the ten concubines Absalom took (16:22; Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Joab himself will later face justice for this and other killings (1 Kings 2:5–6, 28–34), though Solomon names Abner and Amasa, not Absalom.

a: raised a huge pile of stones over him
p: A heap of stones marked the grave of the shamed: Achan and the king of Ai were buried the same way.
b: Achan, who stole what was devoted to God, was stoned, and they raised over him "a great heap of stones" (Joshua 7:26), and so was the king of Ai, hanged on a tree and then buried under stones at the city gate (Joshua 8:29). Absalom, who hung on a tree, gets the same burial, in a pit in the forest. The contrast with 18:18 is pointed: he built himself a monument in the King's Valley, but lies under a heap of rocks in the woods.

a: every man to his own tent
p: This old phrase meant "to his home." Israel had lived in houses for generations.
b: "Each to his tent" is a survival from Israel's tent-dwelling past and means "each went home" (Judges 7:8; 1 Samuel 13:2). It becomes the rallying cry of revolt against the house of David: "To your tents, Israel!" (20:1; 1 Kings 12:16). Here it marks the collapse of Absalom's army.

a: to this day it is called Absalom's Monument
p: The monument in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley called "Absalom's Tomb" today was built about a thousand years after Absalom.
b: The Hebrew word for monument is yad, literally "hand," a standing stone that keeps a name alive, as Saul set one up at Carmel (1 Samuel 15:12; compare Isaiah 56:5, "a hand and a name"). The King's Valley is mentioned in Genesis 14:17 and was probably near Jerusalem. The tall carved monument in the Kidron Valley now called Yad Avshalom dates from the first century AD and is not Absalom's. For centuries Jewish parents brought children there to throw stones at it, as a lesson about what happens to a son who rebels against his father.

a: take the king the good news
p: The verb basar, "carry good news," is the Hebrew behind the Greek word "gospel."
b: Basar means to bring news, usually good news, and its noun besorah is "news" or the reward for it (4:10; 18:22). Isaiah uses it of the messenger who announces God's victory: "How lovely, on the mountains, are the feet of the herald of good news" (Isaiah 52:7), and the Greek translation of this word gave the New Testament its "gospel." This chapter shows how double-edged news can be: a victory for David is the death of his son. Ahimaaz wants to carry it; Joab knows the king will not hear it as good.

a: Then Joab said to the Cushite
p: A Cushite was a man from the upper Nile, roughly modern Sudan. He may have been a foreign servant in Joab's army.
b: Cush in the Bible is the land south of Egypt, Nubia (Genesis 10:6; Isaiah 18:1–2). Black Africans from Cush served in many ancient armies and courts; a later Cushite official, Ebed-melech, rescues Jeremiah from a cistern (Jeremiah 38:7–13). Joab sends him rather than Ahimaaz, probably because a foreign servant could carry bad news without risking the fate of the messenger who brought David news of Saul's death (1:15; 4:10). The narrator never gives his name, but he delivers the truth faithfully.

a: Ahimaaz ran by the road through the Jordan plain and got past the Cushite
p: Ahimaaz took the road along the Jordan valley, longer but flatter, and outran the Cushite on the hill road.
b: Hakkikkar, "the round, the circuit," is the name for the Jordan valley floor (Genesis 13:10). The Cushite apparently took the direct route over the hills of Gilead; Ahimaaz chose the level road and arrived first. He was known for his running (18:27), and for his eagerness, but as 18:29 shows, he had nothing to say when he arrived.

a: David was sitting between the two gates
t: A city gate with two gates
p: City gates in this period had an outer and an inner gate with chambers between, and a room above.
b: Excavated gates from Iron Age towns such as Dan, Megiddo and Gezer had a passage with chambers on each side, and often an outer gate and an inner gate. David waits in the space between, where elders usually sat to hear cases. The lookout climbs to the roof of the gate tower. The "room above the gate" (18:33) where David goes to weep was part of the same structure.

a: Is it peace for the young man, for Absalom?
p: Ahimaaz greeted the king with "Peace!" The king's only question is whether Absalom has shalom.
b: Shalom means safety and wholeness. Ahimaaz shouts it as his first word (18:28), meaning the battle is won. David's question takes up the same word and narrows it to one person: is it shalom for the young man? Absalom's name contains the word too: Avshalom, "my father is peace." David asks twice, to each runner (18:29, 32). Ahimaaz dodges; the Cushite tells the truth politely.

a: The king shook
p: In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 19:1, and the rest of chapter 19 is numbered one higher.
b: English Bibles follow the verse division of the Latin Vulgate here; Hebrew Bibles begin chapter 19 with David's cry. So English 18:33 is Hebrew 19:1, and English 19:1–43 is Hebrew 19:2–44. The site uses the English numbering. The verb wayyirgaz, "he shook," means to tremble with strong feeling, fear or anger or grief (Genesis 45:24; Isaiah 32:10).

a: Oh, if only I had died in your place, I myself!
t: "If only I had died in your place"
p: David's cry is one of the most famous laments in literature. Readers hear grief, guilt and love together.
b: David says "my son" five times in this verse alone. The Talmud counts eight times across 18:33 and 19:4 and says that with seven he raised Absalom up from the seven levels of Gehinnom, and with the eighth brought him into the world to come (Sotah 10b). Literary readers hear guilt as well as grief: Nathan had said the sword would not leave David's house (12:10). Many Christian readers note David's wish to die in his son's place, and contrast it with the gospel, where the Father gives his Son for rebels (Romans 5:8). Moses (Exodus 32:32) and Paul (Romans 9:3) also offered themselves in the place of others. The cry has shaped later art, from Renaissance choral music (a motet attributed to Josquin, and Thomas Tomkins) to William Faulkner's novel Absalom, Absalom!
